title: Does slime facilitate invasion? Differences in exploratory behaviour to slime cues in native Tanychlamys indica and invasive Lissachatina fulica
content:
ABSTRACT
Terrestrial gastropods fulfil pivotal ecological roles, yet numerous species have emerged as high-impact invaders, producing significant consequences for biodiversity, agriculture and human health. While their ecological effects are well documented, the behavioural strategies employed by these invasive species remain comparatively underexplored. Given their limited sensory modalities, chemical communication mediated through slime is central to gastropod behavioural ecology. This study investigated open-area exploratory behaviour in the invasive giant African land snail (Lissachatina fulica) and the native horntail snail (Tanychlamys indica), both collected from sympatric habitats and observed under controlled laboratory conditions. Juvenile and adult individuals of each species were exposed to homospecific and heterospecific slime cues. Results revealed contrasting interspecific responses, such as T. indica, which exhibited suppressed exploration in the presence of heterospecific slime across life stages, suggesting potential spatial displacement and reduced activity. In contrast, adult L. fulica showed enhanced exploratory activity upon encountering heterospecific slime, consistent with a facilitative interaction, whereas juveniles showed minimal sensitivity to both homospecific and heterospecific chemical cues. Asymmetric responses to slime-borne chemical cues between native and invasive gastropods may drive competitive exclusion of T. indica, cascading through food webs to disrupt predator–prey dynamics and threaten ecosystem functioning, while heightened exploration by invasive L. fulica in response to native cues highlights opportunities for synthetic slime-mimicking decoys to divert snails from crops or concentrate them in baited traps. Ultimately, this chemical dialogue in slime not only guides gastropod behaviour but may silently script the outcome of biological invasions.
